To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the epigenetic regulation of gene expression is a critical mechanism of brain development and plasticity in response and adaptation to stress.

(1) the adult and developing brains of both sexes are highly plastic and responsive to stressors, (2) the brain is a key mediator of the stress response and its effects, (3) the sex of the individual and sex of the stressor are critical determinants of brain and behavioral responses to stress, and (4) the epigenetic mechanisms that mediate these responses include genomic, epigenomic, and non-coding RNA alterations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobiology of stress and adaptation and how it differs between the sexes.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the brain is not just the organ that perceives and interprets stress; rather, the brain itself can be the object of stress, and the effects of stress are not just on brain structure and function, but on the brain's ability to regulate the entire body.
the brain-body communication system is highly responsive to stress and is influenced by the sex of the organism, the timing and type of stressor, and the duration of the stressor.
we are studying epigenetic mechanisms that mediate the effects of sex hormones on the brain and behavior, and how the environment can alter these epigenetic mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain-body communication system is not a fixed, immutable entity.
stress can have both positive and negative effects on brain and behavior and these effects depend on the timing and nature of the stressor.
the brain is a dynamic, plastic organ that can be modified by stress and that these modifications can have long-term consequences for brain function and health.
